title: Generate–Verify–Repair for Intent‑Driven Network Changes: Controlled Evaluation with a Deterministic Verifier
abstract: We evaluate whether a generate–verify–repair (GVR) pipeline—single‑shot LLM generation followed by a deterministic network verifier and up to one automated repair—reduces accepted unsafe network changes versus LLM‑only generation. In a preregistered paired design (study-hosted-netops-gvr-v1-2026-08-29) we ran N=500 distinct synthetic intents (shared single initial candidate per intent) with generation by gpt-5-mini and adjudication by a deterministic verifier. Results: guarded (GVR) accepted 500/500 final changes; baseline (LLM-only) accepted 496/500 (paired difference = 0.008). The preregistered primary exact conditional McNemar two‑sided test on the discordant pairs (n10 = 4, n01 = 0) yields p = 0.125 (computed as 2 * PBinom(X ≥ 4; n = 4, p = 0.5)). An exploratory paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples; seed = 1729) = [0.002, 0.016]. Repairs were invoked for 4 initial candidates; total model calls used = 504 (500 shared_initial + 4 repair calls). The preregistered templated‑automation comparator was not executed. We report exact contingency counts, the conditional McNemar calculation, a labeled discussion reconciling the preregistered test and the exploratory bootstrap CI, representative artifact‑grounded diagnostics, execution accounting, and concrete reproducibility pointers to the archived execution manifest and master prompt.

sections.introduction: Operator intent→device configuration translation can reduce manual effort, but errors in generated CLI sequences or transient unsafe states can cause outages. Modern large language models (LLMs) show promise for translating human intent to device configuration, yet hallucination and factual errors remain central reliability concerns for operational NetOps. A practical mitigation architecture is generate–verify–repair (GVR): produce a candidate configuration with an LLM, deterministically verify it against encoded workflow and policy rules, and, if verification fails, run a bounded automated repair attempt. This paper reports a preregistered, artifact‑grounded paired experiment that asks: Does a GVR pipeline (LLM → deterministic verifier → up to one automated repair) produce fewer accepted unsafe changes than LLM‑only generation on a standardized synthetic NetOps intent workload? We contribute: (1) a preregistered paired trial (N=500 paired intents) executed end‑to‑end with archived artifacts; (2) a concise, artifact‑grounded description of generation, verifier semantics, and the bounded repair loop; (3) reconciled confirmatory inference (two‑sided conditional exact McNemar) and exploratory paired bootstrap CI descriptions with an explicit small‑discordant‑count caveat; and (4) execution accounting, representative validator traces, and a discussion of verifier blind spots and practical external‑validity limits.
sections.related_work: Three converging literatures motivate this study. First, surveys and system papers document active interest in LLM‑assisted NetOps tasks including intent translation, configuration generation, AIOps, and multi‑agent orchestration; these works emphasize hallucination and factual errors as deployment barriers [doi:10.1002/nem.2313, https://openalex.org/W4411735779, https://openalex.org/W4413757586]. Second, tool‑augmented and agentic LLM architectures that invoke external verifiers, simulators, or validators have been proposed as a route to operational reliability; deterministic configuration verifiers (e.g., Batfish and distributed verifiers) can check ordering, availability/group constraints, and final‑state properties before deployment [https://openalex.org/W4413757123, https://openalex.org/W4403443637]. Third, methodological work on generate–validate–repair and RAG/tool‑augmented LLM evaluation stresses standardized evaluation practices and the need to quantify verifier coverage and operational costs [https://openalex.org/W4403443637]. Prior empirical evaluations vary in scale; controlled, preregistered paired trials that run identical generator outputs under guarded and unguarded conditions with a deterministic adjudicator are limited, motivating our paired design.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and sampling: The study was preregistered (study-hosted-netops-gvr-v1-2026-08-29). The primary estimand is the paired success‑rate difference (GVR − baseline) over N = 500 distinct intents stratified across 10 synthetic topology profiles. Sampling seeds and the deterministic task generator were frozen per the preregistration. Planned confirmatory test: the two‑sided conditional exact McNemar on discordant pairs; exploratory descriptor: paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples; bootstrap_seed = 1729). The preregistration also specified maximum_model_calls = 1000 and maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1.
Generation and orchestration semantics: For each intent a single shared_initial_generation candidate was produced by the declared model (gpt-5-mini). The GVR controller validated the shared candidate with the deterministic verifier; if verification failed the controller issued at most one automated repair prompt to the same model. The baseline accepted the shared candidate without verifier‑driven repair. The execution manifest and raw results (execution/raw_results.jsonl) are archived in the evidence bundle.
Deterministic verifier semantics (artifact‑grounded): The primary verifier (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) executes a fixed pipeline: (i) syntactic parsing/normalization to canonical commands; (ii) workflow and required‑sequence checks (patterns such as must_be_down_for_fields and all_down_before_any_field_change); (iii) availability/group constraints (exactly_active, minimum_active_in_groups); (iv) dependency and paired‑field enforcement (paired MTU changes, equal_final_fields); and (v) final‑state comparison to the task expected_final_state. Any nonempty violation set yields fail. Per‑episode the verifier emits normalized_configuration, observed_touched_field_count, parsed_command_count, required_command_count, violation list, and boolean valid. Representative validator_trace JSON objects are archived under execution/scoring/ and described in the execution_manifest.
Repair loop and bounded policy: The repair prompt template supplied the original intent abstraction, the verifier violation codes with brief descriptions, and a constrained request for a corrected canonical CLI sequence. At most one repair attempt was permitted per failed shared_initial candidate; a repaired candidate was accepted only if the verifier returned valid. This bounded design isolates the marginal effect of a single repair and limits model‑call overhead (preregistered). The execution/provider_call_audit shows stage_counts: shared_initial_generation = 500, repair = 4 and hosted_model_call_event_count = 504 (see analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json).
Statistical procedures and exact McNemar implementation: Confirmatory inference used the conditional exact McNemar test implemented as the two‑sided exact binomial on discordant pairs. Let n = n10 + n01 and k = n10 (discordants favoring GVR). The preregistered two‑sided p‑value is p = 2 * PBinom(X ≥ k; n, 0.5). The paired bootstrap percentile CI (exploratory) resampled paired outcomes (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) and recomputed the paired difference per resample. Missingness policy: the run produced zero failed episodes so the primary complete‑pair analysis required no imputation.
sections.results:
Execution accounting and contingency counts: completed_episode_count = 1000 (500 intents × 2 conditions). Model calls used = 504 (500 shared_initial + 4 repair calls). analysis/condition_summary reports baseline successes 496/500 (0.992) and guarded successes 500/500 (1.000). The paired contingency table (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv) is n11 = 496, n10 = 4, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Repairs were invoked on 4 initial candidates; all four repaired candidates passed the verifier and correspond to the four discordant pairs (n10 = 4). Mean model calls per accepted change ≈ 504/500 = 1.008; repair_invocations = 4.
Confirmatory test (preregistered): Observed discordants n = 4 with k = n10 = 4. Using the conditional exact McNemar formula p = 2 * PBinom(X ≥ 4; n = 4, p = 0.5). Here PBinom(X ≥ 4; n = 4, p = 0.5) = (1/16), so p = 2 * (1/16) = 0.125. Because this exact conditional test is the preregistered decision rule, we do not claim confirmatory statistical significance.
Exploratory paired bootstrap CI: The paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples; seed = 1729) for the paired difference = [0.002, 0.016] (analysis/analysis_log.jsonl records parameters). As pre‑specified the bootstrap is exploratory: with near‑ceiling margins and only four discordants the bootstrap percentile CI can exclude zero while the conditional McNemar is non‑significant; this arises from differing conditioning and small‑sample instability in the discordant cells.
Representative repaired example (artifact‑grounded): One repaired episode (task_id = task-000004) required a safe transfer pattern (pattern = safe_access_service_transfer, difficulty = very_hard). The shared_initial candidate (execution/responses/task-000004-shared-initial.txt) initially violated a group availability constraint (exactly_active on interfaces edge1/edge2). The GVR repair prompt produced a corrected sequence that satisfied the verifier; the successful validator_trace for the guarded episode is archived at execution/scoring/task-000004-guarded.json. Representative scoring JSON artifacts with validator_trace entries for multiple tasks are archived under execution/scoring/.
Cost proxies and stage accounting: Provider call audit (analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json) shows hosted_model_call_event_count = 504, cache_hit_count = 0, cache_miss_count = 504, and stage_counts mapping shared_initial_generation = 500, repair = 4. These counts quantify the incremental generation cost of the bounded repair policy. We did not measure wall‑clock runtime for the verifier in this run; verifier runtime instrumentation is a recommended operational next step.
Missingness and deviations: complete_pair_count = 500; no episodes failed or were excluded. No deviations from the preregistration were recorded in analysis/results.json. The preregistered templated‑automation comparator was not executed (see Disclosure); that unexecuted arm prevents application of the original two‑test Bonferroni familywise plan as preregistered.
sections.discussion:
Interpretation under preregistered rules: The GVR pipeline prevented four verifier‑detectable unsafe initial candidates that baseline would have accepted. Under the preregistered exact conditional McNemar (p = 0.125) this difference is not confirmatory. The exploratory bootstrap CI excludes zero but should be interpreted cautiously because small discordant counts and near‑ceiling success rates reduce inferential stability and frequentist coverage for percentile bootstrap intervals in this regime. We therefore present both inferential perspectives and follow the preregistered conditional McNemar as the primary decision rule.
Why the inferential approaches diverge: The conditional exact McNemar conditions on the observed marginal totals and evaluates the binomial tail of discordant outcomes; with n = 4 and k = 4 this yields p = 0.125. The paired bootstrap resamples paired outcomes without fixing margins and produces an empirical distribution of paired differences; when paired outcomes are almost all concordant, resampling variability can produce a non‑zero lower CI bound even though the conditional test is non‑significant. Practitioners should treat bootstrap intervals as exploratory descriptors in high‑ceiling, low‑discordant contexts.
Verifier coverage, blind spots, and operational limits: The deterministic verifier enforces canonical syntax normalization, required sequencing, availability/group constraints, dependency/pair rules, and exact final‑state equality to the task expected_final_state. It does not model vendor‑specific CLI semantics, hardware timing effects, control‑plane convergence, or side effects outside the encoded rule set. Passing this verifier is therefore necessary in our experimental safety definition but not sufficient for all real‑world hazards; expanded verifier fidelity (vendor semantics, timing/convergence models) is needed before production automation.
Threats to validity: Internal validity is strong (preregistered pairing, fixed seeds, zero missing pairs). Construct validity is limited by verifier abstractions and synthetic device templates. External validity is constrained by single‑model scope (gpt-5-mini) and synthetic topologies. Conclusion validity was affected by realized margins: the preregistered power plan assumed a larger baseline discordance; the observed baseline (0.992) produced only four discordants and reduced realized sensitivity. These limitations are enumerated in the archived manifest and preregistration record.
sections.conclusion: In a preregistered paired trial (N = 500) using gpt-5-mini and a deterministic verifier, a generate–verify–repair pipeline repaired four verifier‑detectable unsafe initial candidates at modest model‑call cost (4 repairs; model_calls_used = 504). The paired difference = 0.008 yields an exploratory bootstrap 95% CI [0.002, 0.016], while the preregistered exact conditional McNemar test (n10 = 4, n01 = 0) yields p = 0.125; under the preregistered decision rule we do not claim confirmatory significance. Deterministic verification plus a bounded repair loop can remove verifier‑detectable unsafe outputs with low overhead in synthetic settings; broader operational claims require expanded verifier fidelity, adversarial NetOps evaluation, multi‑model replication, and execution of the preregistered templated comparator. All primary execution and analysis artifacts cited here are archived in the evidence bundle for independent verification; consult the execution_manifest for explicit artifact paths and the human‑readable verifier traces under execution/scoring/.

disclosure_statement: This study was executed autonomously after an explicit autonomy lock. Generation model used in the archived run: gpt-5-mini (declared_model_version recorded in execution/model_configuration.json). Orchestration adapter family: hosted_netops_gvr_v1 using the hosted provider recorded as 'openai_responses'. Key automated components recorded in the run: deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 (task synthesis), deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (primary deterministic verifier/scorer), and the GVR controller implementing shared_initial_generation plus an automated single‑repair step (maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1). The design, preregistration (study-hosted-netops-gvr-v1-2026-08-29), code generation, execution, analysis, manuscript drafting, autonomous peer review, and revision were performed autonomously after the autonomy lock; no human manually edited or rewrote manuscript technical content after that lock. The immutable initial master prompt is archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256: 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). The evidence bundle includes execution/execution_manifest.json, which enumerates every archived artifact path and its SHA‑256 hash; the full hash manifest and the human‑readable validator traces (execution/scoring/), the task_manifest entries (execution/task_manifest.jsonl), raw responses (execution/responses/), and scoring outputs are listed there. Primary high‑level execution quantities reported here (N = 500 complete pairs; model_calls_used = 504; repair calls = 4; paired counts n11 = 496, n10 = 4, n01 = 0, n00 = 0) are derived from archived execution and analysis artifacts in the bundle. The preregistered templated‑automation comparator was not executed in this archived run; that unexecuted arm means the originally preregistered two‑test Bonferroni familywise plan could not be fully applied.
limitations: Synthetic tasks and topology profiles were used (synthetic_topologies_v1 and synthetic_device_configs_v1); external validity to production hardware, vendor‑specific CLIs, live telemetry, and control‑plane timing effects is untested.
Only a single generation model (gpt-5-mini) was evaluated; multi‑model generality and replication remain to be established.

Safety in this experiment is defined relative to deterministic_netops_validator_v5’s encoded rule set (syntactic parsing/normalization, required‑sequence/workflow‑policy checks, protected‑interface rules, group and availability constraints, dependency‑rule enforcement, and final‑state comparison to the task expected_final_state). Passing this verifier is necessary for the experiment’s outcome but not sufficient for all real‑world safety properties.

The preregistered power plan targeted an absolute paired increase ≈ 0.08 (8 percentage points). The observed baseline success rate (496/500 = 0.992) produced only four discordant pairs, substantially reducing realized power relative to the preregistered assumption and limiting confirmatory sensitivity.

The preregistered templated‑automation comparator (secondary confirmatory arm) was not executed; therefore the preregistered multiplicity plan (two confirmatory tests with Bonferroni correction) could not be fully applied and the familywise error interpretation is partial.
